content: Dental sealants were first introduced in the 1960s as a preventive measure against dental caries, particularly targeting the pits and fissures on the occlusal surfaces of teeth. These sealants function by creating a physical barrier that inhibits bacterial growth, which is a primary cause of dental decay. Research has demonstrated that fissure sealants are effective in reducing caries in children and adolescents when compared to no sealant application. However, the degree of effectiveness may vary depending on the baseline caries incidence within the population being studied. This review is an update of previous reviews conducted in 2004, 2008, and 2013. The primary objective of this review was to evaluate and compare the effectiveness of different types of fissure sealants in preventing caries on the occlusal surfaces of permanent teeth in children and adolescents. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to August 3, 2016. Additional searches were performed on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing trials. No restrictions were placed on the language or publication date of the studies. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared sealants with either no sealant or a different type of sealant material for preventing caries on the occlusal surfaces of premolar or molar teeth in children and adolescents up to 20 years of age. Studies were required to have a minimum follow-up period of 12 months. Trials comparing compomers to resins or composites were excluded. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. Outcomes were reported as odds ratios (OR) or risk ratios (RR) for the presence or absence of caries on occlusal surfaces, and mean differences (MD) were used for mean caries increment. All results were presented with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were conducted using a random-effects model when more than three trials were available; otherwise, a fixed-effect model was used. The GRADE approach was employed to assess the quality of the evidence. A total of 38 trials involving 7,924 children were included in this review, with seven new trials (1,693 participants) added since the last update. Fifteen trials evaluated resin-based sealants versus no sealant (3,620 participants across 14 studies, plus 575 tooth pairs in one study). Three trials assessed glass ionomer sealants versus no sealant (905 participants), and 24 trials compared one type of sealant to another (4,146 participants). The age range of participants was 5 to 16 years. Most trials did not report participants' baseline exposure to fluoride or caries prevalence. For resin-based sealants compared to no sealant, moderate-quality evidence showed that second-, third-, and fourth-generation resin-based sealants effectively prevented caries in the first permanent molars of children aged 5 to 10 years. At 24 months of follow-up, the odds ratio for caries prevention was 0.12 (95% CI 0.08 to 0.19) based on seven trials (five from the 1970s and two from the 2010s) involving 1,548 randomized children, with 1,322 children evaluated. Assuming that 16% of control tooth surfaces developed caries over 24 months (160 carious teeth per 1,000), the application of resin-based sealants would reduce the proportion of carious surfaces to 5.2% (95% CI 3.13% to 7.37%). Similarly, if 40% of control tooth surfaces were affected (400 carious teeth per 1,000), sealants would reduce the proportion to 6.25% (95% CI 3.84% to 9.63%). For a baseline caries rate of 70%, the proportion of decayed surfaces in the sealant group would be 19% (95% CI 12.3% to 27.2%). This caries-preventive effect persisted at longer follow-up intervals, although the quality and quantity of evidence diminished. For example, at 48 to 54 months of follow-up, the odds ratio was 0.21 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.28) based on four trials with 482 children evaluated, and the risk ratio was 0.24 (95% CI 0.12 to 0.45) based on 203 children evaluated. However, all trials were at high risk of bias for blinding of outcome assessment, as it is not feasible to blind assessors in sealant studies due to the visible nature of the intervention. For glass ionomer sealants compared to no sealant, three studies provided inconclusive results at 24 months, with very low-quality evidence. When comparing one type of sealant to another, the relative effectiveness of different sealant materials remains uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. A total of 24 trials directly compared two different sealant materials, but these comparisons varied in terms of the types of sealants assessed, the outcome measures chosen, and the duration of follow-up. Adverse events were assessed in only four trials, and no adverse events were reported in any of these studies. In conclusion, resin-based sealants applied to the occlusal surfaces of permanent molars are effective in preventing caries in children and adolescents. Moderate-quality evidence indicates that resin-based sealants reduce caries by 11% to 51% compared to no sealant at 24 months of follow-up. Similar benefits were observed at time points up to 48 months, although the quality and quantity of evidence decreased with longer follow-up. There is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of glass ionomer sealants or to compare the relative effectiveness of different types of sealants. Information on adverse effects is limited, but no adverse events were reported in the studies that assessed them. Further research with extended follow-up periods is necessary to strengthen the evidence base.
